title: Hollow back construction
subtitle: Building a paper tube spine that lets the book open flat
excerpt: A hollow back separates the spine covering from the sewn text block so the book opens flat without straining the binding. The hollow is a tube of paper glued to the outside of the spine liner, leaving a gap between the tube and the book block.
sourceNotes: Douglas Cockerell, Bookbinding and the Care of Books (1901), chapter on spine construction: detailed description of hollow-back and tight-back spine options, with notes on when each is appropriate.

glossaryTerms.definition: A spine construction where the covering material is attached to a paper tube glued to the outside of the book block, leaving a gap between tube and text block so the book opens flat.
A spine construction where the covering material is glued directly to the spine of the sewn book block, producing a rounded back that opens only partially flat.
A strip of mull or super glued to the outside of the sewn text block to consolidate and reinforce the spine before covering.

content.text: is the standard spine construction for a book intended to open flat. A paper tube sits between the book block and the spine covering: when the book opens, the covering stays still and the text block rolls away from it inside the tube. The alternative, the
, glues covering directly to the spine and is only appropriate for books that do not need to open flat or for very thick, stiff bindings.

items.name: Kraft paper, 80-120 gsm
items.notes: Two strips per book, each exactly the width of the spine and three times its length, cut with the grain running head to tail.

items.name: PVA, acid-free
items.notes: Thin slightly with water to a milk consistency so it spreads evenly without lumps.

items.name: Paste brush, 50 mm flat
items.notes: For spreading adhesive over the kraft strip.

items.name: Bone folder
items.notes: For burnishing the tube onto the spine and pressing glued layers flat.

items.name: Craft knife + metal ruler
items.notes: For trimming the kraft strip cleanly to exact width.

content.text: Measure and cut the kraft strip

Measure the spine width of the text block precisely with a ruler. Cut a strip of kraft paper exactly that width and three times the spine length, grain running head-to-tail. Grain direction is critical: a tube built against the grain will try to unbend itself and will eventually delaminate. To check the grain, flex the strip gently in both directions and cut parallel to the direction that bends easily.
Apply the first layer to the spine liner
Lay the sewn text block spine-up. The

(mull or super) should already be in place and dry. Brush a thin, even coat of diluted PVA onto the first third of the kraft strip. Press this section firmly onto the spine liner, centred from head to tail. Rub with the bone folder through a scrap of waxed paper to bond it without slipping. Leave the remaining two thirds of the strip unglued for now.

When the first section is nearly dry but still slightly tacky, fold the strip back on itself so the free end runs back along the spine and aligns with the head and tail. The fold creates the outer face of the tube. Then fold it back once more so the last third lies on top of the first. Brush PVA onto the inner face of this final layer and press it down onto the outer face of the first layer. The three layers now form a three-ply paper tube. Burnish the whole tube firmly with the bone folder. The tube should be stiff, even, and square along its length.
Allow to dry under light pressure

Stand the book on its tail and allow the tube to dry in open air for 30 minutes. Avoid pressing the tube tightly against the spine at this stage: the tube needs to remain separate from the book block except at the single glued strip at its base. Once dry, the book should open and the tube should separate cleanly from the spine each time.

The outer face of the tube is the surface the spine covering attaches to. When making the case, glue the covering material to the tube exterior in the same way you would to a tight-back spine, but only to the tube, not to the book block beneath. The book is now ready for casing-in: the text block drops into the case with its boards glued to the covering boards, and the spine covering sits on the tube with no adhesion to the book block itself.

items.symptom: The tube delaminates after a few openings
items.cause: The grain of the kraft strip ran across the spine rather than head-to-tail, so the paper tries to curl against the tube shape.
items.fix: Rebuild with a new strip, checking that the grain runs parallel to the spine length before cutting.

items.symptom: The book block and tube do not separate when the book opens
items.cause: PVA crept beyond the first third of the strip during gluing.
items.fix: On future tubes, mask the free two-thirds of the strip with a scrap of waxed paper before brushing adhesive. For a finished binding, gentle humidification from inside the covers can soften the bond enough to free the tube.

items.symptom: The tube is uneven, with one end wider than the other
items.cause: The kraft strip was cut slightly wider than the spine, or the folds were not aligned square to the head and tail.
items.fix: Trim the tube to exact width with the craft knife against a metal ruler once dry. Remeasure before cutting.
